slides.transcript: Welcome to Optical Circuit Switching for AI and Hyperscale Data Centers. We begin with the architectural idea behind an optical circuit: establishing a path for light between selected endpoints. Across five modules, you'll connect that idea to physical switch technologies, deployed networks, emerging applications, and the open ecosystem. This first module gives you the boundary conditions you'll need throughout the course. Keep one question in mind: which functions does the optical path provide, and which functions still belong elsewhere?

slides.title: What you will be able to explain
objectives: Explain how an optical circuit differs from per-packet forwarding.
Locate the electrical endpoints and optical switching boundary.
Relate efficiency, latency and upgrade flexibility to physical limits.
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you'll be able to describe an optical circuit without confusing it with a packet switch. You'll identify where optical-to-electrical conversion is avoided, and where electrical processing still occurs. You'll also explain why a bufferless component can reduce one source of delay without making a whole network contention-free. The goal is a practical vocabulary for the technology and deployment choices that follow.

slides.title: Locate the optical switching boundary

figure.alt: Electrical endpoints flank a transparent optical circuit, with the service boundary explicitly marked.
figure.caption: The optical switching path stays transparent; electrical processing remains at surrounding endpoints.
figure.source_scope: M1 / How OCS Works; Packet Handling marker

entries.text: Light stays optical through the switching stage

slides.transcript:
Optical circuit switching, or OCS, establishes a selected optical connection between ports. The signal remains light through that switching path. Electrical packet switching, or EPS, instead uses electronic logic to make forwarding decisions about packets. When an optical link enters an electrical switch, a receiver converts the signal to electrical form; transmission onto another optical link converts it back to light. This is optical-electrical-optical, or OEO, conversion.

Avoiding that conversion at a selected network stage can remove its electronic processing and associated power demand. The transmitting and receiving endpoints still need their own electronics. A hybrid network can therefore retain packet switching around an optical circuit layer. The useful comparison is between complete architectures with equivalent requirements, rather than between an isolated optical component and an entire electrical network.

slides.title: A dedicated circuit has a specific job

figure.alt: Four endpoints share an optical switch; a second connection request reveals the difference between circuit connectivity and packet services.
figure.caption: A circuit directs light between selected ports; traffic scheduling and packet services belong elsewhere in the system.

entries.text: The circuit redirects light; it does not read packets.
Packet services remain in the surrounding electrical systems.
A second demand needs a supported allocation.

slides.transcript:
Start with four endpoints and one optical circuit switch. The controller selects a connection from endpoint A to endpoint B. Inside the switch, the optical signal follows that established path. The switch does not need to read each packet to decide where the signal goes.

The electrical endpoints still generate and receive traffic. Packet inspection, buffering, and quality of service can exist in those surrounding systems. They are not functions supplied by the transparent optical path itself.

Now endpoint C also needs to communicate with B. The optical switch does not magically combine two independent demands onto the same dedicated connection. The broader system must decide how to allocate its available connectivity and when to change it.

This gives us two distinct activities: selecting a circuit, then transferring data through it. Bufferless operation removes packet queuing inside the optical switch. It does not promise that an entire network is free of contention. Keep that boundary in mind whenever you evaluate an OCS benefit.

slides.title: Five dimensions of the tradeoff

figure.alt: A five-row OCS versus electrical packet switching comparison.
figure.caption: Compare latency, power, packet services, rate transparency and optical reach.
figure.source_scope: M1 / How OCS Works / five labeled markers

entries.text: No packet queue in the OCS

slides.transcript:
A circuit changes several design decisions at once. First, it avoids packet queuing inside the transparent optical switch, while propagation and endpoint delays remain. Second, removing an electrical processing stage can lower power, but the controller, actuation and transceivers still consume energy. Third, packet inspection and quality of service must be provided by systems that can interpret the traffic.

Fourth, a transparent path can support different data rates and protocols within its optical operating limits. Fifth, loss accumulates along the path because a passive optical switch does not regenerate the signal. These properties explain why optical and electrical switching often work together. A good design assigns each function to a component that can perform it, then checks the combined result against the application's needs.

slides.title: Separate a circuit decision from packet decisions

bullets.text: Select and verify the port-to-port circuit.
Carry light through the established path.
Coordinate competing demand in the wider system.

slides.transcript:
A controller decides which ports should be connected. That connection can remain useful for a communication phase, a job, or a longer deployment interval. While it is established, the optical path carries the signal without deciding where each individual packet should go.

Suppose several senders need the same receiver at once. A circuit alone does not schedule those competing demands. The design may allocate different connections, wait for a different interval, or use surrounding packet switching and traffic control. This is why circuit setup time and data-transfer latency are different measurements. One describes changing connectivity. The other describes using an established path. Keeping the two separate prevents a fast transfer path from being mistaken for instantaneous reconfiguration.

slides.title: Budget the light from transmitter to receiver

figure.alt: Four progressively smaller qualitative power bars accompany a transmitter, optical switch, connectors and receiver.
figure.caption: Each element consumes part of the optical budget; acceptable paths depend on the complete link.
figure.source_scope: M1 / Insertion Loss; Benefits and Limitations

entries.text: Illustrative relative power — no numeric loss scale
Every passive element contributes to the link budget.
Allowed hop count depends on the complete optical design.

slides.transcript:
Insertion loss is the reduction in optical power caused by introducing a component into a path. Fibers, connectors and optical switches all contribute to the link budget. The receiver must still receive a usable signal after those losses, with an appropriate operating margin.

The source course emphasizes that practical optical fabrics often avoid long cascades of switches. Treat that as a design implication, not a universal limit of exactly one or two hops. The allowable path depends on the components, wavelength, transceiver capability and complete optical budget. Adding amplification or regeneration changes the architecture and its tradeoffs. Start with the end-to-end path that the application requires, then establish whether every permitted circuit can meet the optical conditions.

slides.title: Evaluate a proposed speed upgrade

bullets.text: Retain the transparent switching layer across endpoint generations.
Validate wavelength, optical bandwidth, loss and transceiver compatibility.
Protocol transparency does not supply packet inspection or QoS.

slides.transcript:
A data-rate-agnostic optical path does not decode the bit rate to decide where the light travels. That can allow an operator to update electrical endpoints while retaining the optical switching layer. It is an attractive separation of upgrade cycles.

It is not a promise that any future transceiver works with any installed optical path. Engineers still verify supported wavelengths, optical bandwidth, connector and fiber arrangements, insertion loss, and receiver requirements. The same caution applies to protocol transparency: carrying a signal does not supply the protocol's packet services. A useful design question is therefore, what must change at the endpoints, and what evidence supports retaining the optical path? That question turns a broad benefit into a testable upgrade plan.

slides.title: A transparent path with explicit limits
items: OCS selects optical connectivity; EPS supplies per-packet forwarding.
Efficiency and rate transparency are architectural opportunities.
Contention, optical loss and endpoint functions still need engineering.
slides.transcript:
The central idea is now in place. Optical circuit switching changes connectivity while keeping the signal in the optical domain through the switch. Its lack of packet buffers removes queuing at that component. It does not remove all sources of delay or contention in a network.

The strongest benefits appear when an architecture can avoid an electrical stage and keep useful circuits established long enough to justify reconfiguration. Optical loss and endpoint compatibility remain practical constraints. Use these boundaries as a checklist whenever you encounter a claim about lower power, faster links, or easier upgrades.

slides.title: The OCS Technology Landscape
slides.subtitle: Match the physical switching mechanism to a workload and optical budget.
slides.transcript: Module two examines the OCS technology landscape. Optical circuit switching describes a function, but several different physical mechanisms can provide it. Some move fibers or mirrors. Others control polarization or guide light through a chip. We'll compare those mechanisms using the same questions: how quickly must connectivity change, how many ports are needed, and what optical and power constraints apply? These questions help you identify a good physical fit without treating any technology family as a universal winner.

slides.title: What you will be able to explain
objectives: Identify six technology families and the role of hybrid designs.
Compare actuation, switching time, radix, loss and power.
Choose evaluation criteria for a stable or changing workload.
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you'll recognize the operating principle behind robotic, MEMS, liquid-crystal, piezoelectric, silicon-photonic and metasurface approaches. You'll also understand why hybrid designs combine mechanisms. More importantly, you'll be able to separate a family-level description from a particular device specification. A technology name does not guarantee a switching time or port count.

slides.title: Six ways to establish a light path

figure.alt: Six cards describe robotic, MEMS, liquid crystal, piezoelectric, silicon-photonic and metasurface switching.
figure.caption: Start with the physical mechanism, then evaluate the specific implementation.

entries.text: Hybrid systems combine mechanisms; they are not a seventh physical principle.

slides.transcript:
The six families organize the physical choices. Robotic mechanisms move and connect fibers. Micro-electro-mechanical systems, usually called MEMS, tilt small mirrors to steer light through free space. Liquid-crystal devices alter optical polarization under electrical control. Piezoelectric actuators deform a material to produce precise motion.

Silicon photonics routes light through small waveguides on a chip, using effects such as electro-optic or thermo-optic phase changes. Metasurfaces use tunable sub-wavelength structures to control the optical wavefront. Hybrid designs combine mechanisms to balance their strengths. This classification describes how light is routed. It does not by itself establish a complete system's scale, loss, speed, lifetime or operational maturity.

slides.title: Mechanical movement spans very different timescales

bullets.text: Physical fiber movement; often suited to infrequent reconfiguration.
Small tilting mirrors; established high-port-count implementations.
Voltage-driven deformation; timing depends on device and settling.

slides.transcript:
Robotic patching resembles an automated fiber patch panel. It can support large connectivity inventories, and a latched physical connection may hold without actuation power. Reconfiguration can take seconds to minutes. That can be useful for provisioning or infrequent changes, but it does not fit every workload.

MEMS mirrors move much smaller structures and commonly offer millisecond-scale reconfiguration with substantial port counts. Piezoelectric actuation uses voltage-driven deformation for precise positioning. Depending on the device and its settling requirements, implementations can span microsecond-to-millisecond behavior. The original material uses inconsistent timing descriptions for this family, so the responsible comparison is the measured device specification. Include settling, verification and system coordination when deciding whether a mechanism meets the required switching window.

slides.title: Solid-state does not mean one speed or power profile

figure.alt: Thermo-optic and electro-optic actuation both lead to refractive-index and phase changes through different physical controls.
figure.caption: Electro-optic and thermo-optic actuation differ; integration does not remove the optical budget.
figure.source_scope: M2 / MEMS vs. Silicon Photonics original video

entries.text: Phase control changes interference and the output path.

slides.transcript:
Liquid crystals manipulate polarization without mechanically steering a mirror. Silicon photonics can change the path within integrated waveguides. Metasurfaces control a wavefront using many small tunable elements. All avoid some forms of mechanical movement, but their operating characteristics remain different.

Within silicon photonics, electro-optic and thermo-optic actuation are especially important to distinguish. Electrical changes and thermal changes do not have identical response times or holding-power requirements. Cascaded switching elements can also add optical loss as a design scales. Semiconductor optical amplifiers may compensate some loss, but introduce their own power, noise and integration considerations. Evaluate the complete implementation rather than assuming that chip-scale integration automatically supplies high radix, low loss and the fastest possible switching at once.

slides.title: Compare constraints, not isolated rankings
slides.transcript:
Use a comparison matrix to expose questions, not to declare a permanent ranking. Port count, also called radix, tells you how much connectivity the switch can expose. Insertion loss tells you how much optical margin each permitted path consumes. Switching time must cover the relevant transition and settling conditions. Power should distinguish changing a state from maintaining it, while including the surrounding system.

The categories on screen summarize the original technology landscape. Real products can cross those broad categories. Ask for the exact port configuration, wavelength range, path-loss distribution and measurement method. Then compare devices against the same workload and service requirement. A very fast device with insufficient optical margin or connectivity can still be the wrong choice.

slides.title: Choose for the available switching window

figure.alt: Two workload timelines contrast a long stable communication phase with frequent reconfiguration, alongside four selection constraints.
figure.caption: A useful technology choice balances reconfiguration time, useful transfer time, radix, optical loss and power.

entries.text: The connection remains useful after setup.
The same setup occupies more of each short interval.
Timing + radix + optical loss + power + maturity
Choose an implementation that fits the workload.

slides.transcript:
A switching time becomes meaningful only when we compare it with the workload. Consider a cluster whose connections stay useful for a long communication phase. A relatively slow reconfiguration may be acceptable when the system can establish the circuits before that phase begins.

Now consider a different workload that needs new connections much more frequently. If reconfiguration consumes most of the available interval, the useful transfer window shrinks. The same switching mechanism can therefore be a good fit for one workload and a poor fit for another.

Robotic patching, mirror steering, polarization control, material deformation, on-chip routing, and phase steering provide different design options. Their actual timing depends on the implementation. Even within silicon photonics, electro-optic and thermo-optic actuation have different speed and power characteristics.

Do not stop at the fastest number. Check the required port count, the end-to-end optical loss budget, the power used to change and maintain a state, and the maturity of the design. The best physical fit is the one that satisfies these constraints within the workload’s available switching window.

slides.transcript: Module three connects optical switching to current AI data-center deployments. Google's Jupiter and TPU version four examples provide concrete context. We'll preserve the conditions around their results and separate what the optical fabric changes from the functions that remain in electrical switches, controllers and workload software.

objectives: Identify the layer changed by optical interconnect deployment.
Explain Cube-to-Cube connectivity in the TPUv4 example.
Distinguish physical reconnection from complete workload recovery.
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you'll be able to locate the optical layer in two very different architectures. One connects groups of packet switches across a data center. Another connects compute Cubes into a configurable accelerator topology. You'll also explain how optical reconnection can help resilience, and why successful application recovery requires more than a new path.

slides.transcript:
In the Jupiter evolution described by the OCP white paper, optical circuit switching helps replace a selected electrical interconnect stage. Electrical switching remains elsewhere in the network. The architecture allows connectivity between blocks to evolve and supports incremental upgrades without tying every stage to the same electronic switching generation.

The cited comparison reports a forty-one percent reduction in network power, a thirty percent reduction in capital expenditure, and five times the throughput. These are results associated with that deployment and its comparison conditions. They are not a guarantee from installing an OCS device in any network. Use the example to understand the mechanism, then evaluate your own topology, traffic, transceivers, redundancy and operating requirements.

entries.text: Trace the functions performed at the interconnect stage.

Rate transparency does not remove the optical link budget.

slides.transcript:
Begin with this simplified fabric. Electrical packet switches connect groups of endpoints through an electrical interconnect stage. Following one optical link through that stage requires optical-to-electrical conversion, packet processing, and conversion back to light.

Now identify the layer that an optical circuit switching architecture changes. We replace the selected interconnect stage with a fabric of configurable optical paths. This is an architectural example, not a port-for-port drawing of a particular production network.

The surrounding electrical switches remain important. They still handle packet functions while the optical fabric provides selected connectivity between them. A controller can revise those connections as the deployment requires. This does not mean that every endpoint has a permanently dedicated path to every other endpoint.

Finally, consider an endpoint speed upgrade. The optical switching path does not interpret the bit rate, so it can avoid the electronic switching limits of the replaced stage. Engineers must still verify transceiver compatibility, optical bandwidth, insertion loss, and the complete link budget. Rate transparency is a valuable property, not a waiver of system engineering.

slides.title: How the TPUv4 optical topology changes

cues.text: Training modern artificial intelligence models requires thousands
of accelerators working in perfect synchronization.
To achieve this,
Google deployed optical circuit switching in their TPU V4 clusters
to dynamically weave these chips into a massive reconfigurable supercomputer.
The foundation of this architecture is called a cube.
Inside a single TPU V4 rack,
there are 16 servers.
Each server hosts 4 TPUs,
resulting in 64 TPUs hardwired together in a 4 by 4 by 4 electrical mesh.
Inside the cube,
all connections are electrical,
but to scale up,
the cube must connect to the broader network.
It does this by extending optical fibers outward across 6 different logical faces.
These optical fibers travel from the cube to 3 distinct groups of OCS devices.
These switch groups correspond to the X,
Y,
and Z dimensions of the network fabric.
When you combine 64 of these cubes together,
you get a super pod.
A full TPUV4 superpod contains exactly 48 MEMS optical circuit switches,
providing connectivity for over 4000 TPUs.
If these connections use traditional electrical switches,
the network topology would be rigidly fixed.
But because this fabric uses optical circuit switching,
the physical network itself is entirely programmable.
A software control plane can dynamically reconfigure the
optical switches on a per job basis.
It logically rearranges the cubes to create custom network topologies
like a Tauruss
that perfectly match the communication patterns of a specific training job.
This flexibility allows operators to logically subdivide the superpod.
Specific groups of cubes can be entirely isolated,
allowing multiple independent jobs
to run simultaneously without any performance or security interference.
The OCS fabric also provides incredible hardware failure resiliency.
If a TPU cube fails,
the control panel detects the fault
and automatically reconfigures the optical mirrors
to completely bypass the failed hardware.
This rapid physical layer recovery restores full
performance without relying on degraded electrical rerouting.
By making the physical connections dynamic,
OCS transforms the network into an active
and highly resilient AI platform.

slides.transcript:
A fixed physical network constrains every job to the same topology. Configurable Cube-to-Cube connectivity gives the controller another option: select a topology that fits the allocated resources and communication pattern. A three-dimensional torus is one important example in the TPU architecture.

This is a physical connectivity decision, coordinated with job placement and system operation. It should not be confused with inspecting and rerouting every packet in the optical switch. Nor does the example imply arbitrary instantaneous topology changes while traffic is active. The controller must respect the available ports, permitted paths, optical conditions and transition process. The value comes from making the physical fabric a resource the system can configure deliberately.

cues.text: As AI and high performance computing systems continue to scale,
hardware failures become a normal operating condition.
Switches,
links,
and optical modules
will inevitably fail.
Traditional network recovery mechanisms rely on software-based rerouting,
which often cannot fully restore performance.
Traffic is squeezed through remaining active paths,
creating bottlenecks that slow down critical workloads.
Optical circuit switching introduces a new approach to resiliency
by making the physical network itself
programmable.
Let us walk through a failure recovery event in an OCS enabled data center.
Imagine a critical spine switch
suddenly fails during a training workload.
The switch goes dark,
completely breaking the physical link for the servers below it.
First,
the software control plane handles failure detection and notification.
The system instantly registers the hardware fault
and initiates the recovery cycle.
Next,
the system performs an optical connections calculation.
Rather than duplicating every single network path,
the architecture utilizes a shared pool of redundant electrical switches
and spare optical paths.
The control plane automatically reconfigures the optical connections
to bypass the faulty component.
This triggers the enforcement phase,
where the optical switch responds by physically redirecting
the light beams to the healthy spare switch.
Once the physical path is set,
the network performs a topology sweep and recovery.
The routing tables update instantly to
recognize the newly established physical connection.
Finally,
we reach application and system capacity recovery.
Unlike traditional rerouting,
optical reconfiguration
restores the intended connectivity
and full available bandwidth.
AI jobs continue running without restarts or prolonged slowdowns,
and they do so at the full fabric capacity.
By enabling automated physical layer recovery,
optical circuit switching transforms the network
from a passive transport layer
into an active resiliency platform.

ACTINA stands for Adaptive Circuit Switching Techniques for AI Networking Architectures. Its OCS-BCube concept explores a multidimensional optical topology for accelerator training, using specialized silicon-photonic, multi-port transceivers. A controller can use workload demand to change wavelength assignments and steer available bandwidth.

Three layers must stay distinct. The physical topology determines possible paths. The workload creates communication demand. The control system chooses how available optical capacity serves that demand. Wavelength reconfiguration changes an allocation supported by the architecture; it does not create arbitrary new fibers. Performance therefore depends on the transceiver design, the prediction or knowledge of traffic, and the overhead of making a change at the right time.

During one iteration, some communicating groups need more bandwidth than others. A traffic-aware controller uses that demand to choose an allocation supported by the architecture. In the source concept, wavelength-reconfigurable transceivers are part of the mechanism that changes this allocation.

cues.text: As AI models grow more complex,
new training architectures like mixture of experts are emerging.
In these models,
a strategy called expert parallelism is central to distributed training.
Expert parallelism requires intense all to all
communication across a distributed group of GPUs.
In fact,
it has the highest communication volume of any major parallelism strategy.
The challenge is that the communicating GPUs and their traffic volumes
change from iteration to iteration.
The exact routing is not known until after the computation phase.
This unpredictability makes it very difficult
to reconfigure an optical switch in advance
without stalling the entire training pipeline.
To solve this,
researchers developed Mixnet,
a hybrid electrical and optical interconnect architecture.
Mixnet divides the network into three
distinct fabric layers to optimize performance.
First,
the local scale-up fabric uses electrical switches to connect
GPUs within the same server or high bandwidth domain.
Second,
the cluster-wide scale-out fabric uses traditional packet
switching to connect servers across the cluster.
Finally,
Mixnet introduces the regional OCS fabric.
This optical layer is entirely dedicated to handling
the massive dynamic communication patterns of expert parallelism.
But how does the system know when to reconfigure the optical switches?
Mixnet relies on two key insights.
First,
expert parallelism communication is highly localized.
Usually,
only a small group of 8 to 32 GPUs participate in an all to all communication phase.
Second,
these traffic patterns only change gradually between iterations.
Because consecutive iterations are so similar,
MixNet can accurately predict the next traffic pattern based on the previous one.
This predictability unlocks a massive performance gain.
MixNet dynamically reconfigures the optical circuit switches
during the computation portion of an iteration.
By the time the GPUs finish their calculations and are ready to talk,
the optical links are already set in place.
There is no waiting.
This hybrid approach perfectly aligns physical
interconnect resources with workload demands.
In simulations,
Nixnet reduced training time for large models by
1.6 times compared to a static packet network.

MixNet studies how that traffic can use a regional optical fabric alongside electrical networks.

Its local electrical fabric serves communication within a server. A global electrical fabric, using technologies such as Ethernet or InfiniBand, supports broader communication including data and pipeline parallelism. The regional optical fabric focuses on expert-parallel traffic. The MixNet idea exploits an overlap opportunity. While accelerators perform computation, the system can prepare regional optical connections for the upcoming communication phase. If the demand prediction is useful and the change completes in time, less of the communication interval is consumed by reconfiguration.

This arrangement depends on coordination. The controller needs a sufficiently accurate view of demand, the optical fabric needs enough capacity, and the transition must fit the available compute window. A prediction error or a longer-than-expected change can reduce the benefit. Hybrid fabrics provide a way to assign traffic according to these properties, rather than forcing every flow through the same mechanism. The 2026 use-case discussion also frames orchestration and spare-resource pooling as system-level requirements.

signals undergo multiple optical,
electrical,
optical conversions.

or qubits.

quantum states cannot be copied or measured without being destroyed.

This preserves the high fidelity required for quantum teleportation
and distributed quantum computing.

through resource disaggregation.

connects servers with pooled resources such as accelerators,
memory,
and storage.

the effective reach of high-speed copper links
continues to shrink at higher signaling rates.

adds unacceptable latency
and power consumption.

because it is inherently rate agnostic,
it allows bandwidth to scale efficiently without reducing port count.
Additionally,
OCS avoids OEO conversion delays and eliminates queuing related latency.
This enables the ultra low latency required
for resource desegregation architectures.
Whether preserving delicate cubits
or accelerating memory,
pure light is the ultimate transport layer.

entries.text: Loss, noise and state fidelity still require verification.

Optical transparency is a property, not an end-to-end guarantee.

slides.transcript:
Quantum networking uses physical quantum states rather than simply reading and retransmitting classical bits. The no-cloning theorem says that an arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be copied perfectly. It is not the statement that every measurement always destroys every state. Measurement effects depend on the state and measurement performed.

A conventional packet switch does not transparently forward an encoded photonic qubit through its usual receive, process and retransmit pipeline. An optical circuit can avoid that classical conversion, making it a useful candidate for quantum interconnection. But loss, noise, phase stability and polarization behavior still matter to the encoding. OCS does not automatically preserve any quantum state under all conditions. The quantum network must validate the entire path and its protocol requirements.

slides.title: Connect resource pools without inventing their semantics

bullets.text: Compose supported compute, memory, storage or accelerator resources.
Provide configurable paths and potentially multiple wavelength channels.
Validate latency, protocols, isolation and endpoint behavior.

slides.transcript:
Resource disaggregation separates pools of compute, memory, storage or accelerators so systems can compose resources for a task. Configurable optical connectivity can support that composition across a larger physical footprint. Avoiding an electrical switching stage may reduce part of the transport overhead.

An optical path does not, by itself, provide cache coherence, memory access semantics, isolation or a suitable latency guarantee. Those functions depend on endpoints, protocols and software. Dense wavelength division multiplexing, or DWDM, carries multiple wavelength channels on a fiber and can help use its capacity efficiently. It does not remove propagation delay or the optical budget. The useful question is which resource-pooling requirement the optical fabric helps satisfy, and which requirements the remaining system must still meet.

slides.subtitle: Connect deployment evidence to interoperable systems and community participation.
slides.transcript: Module five asks what's next for the OCS ecosystem. Production deployments have established important use cases, while research continues to explore new ways to use optical connectivity. Broader adoption depends on more than a switching component. It also needs clear capabilities, consistent control, operational verification and shared evidence. We'll connect those needs to the roles of technology suppliers, systems integrators, operators and the open standards community.

slides.title: What you will be able to explain
objectives: Distinguish deployment evidence from research and planned demonstrations.
Identify the ecosystem roles and their interoperability handoffs.
Choose a practical way to contribute requirements or validation evidence.
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you'll be able to explain why a successful deployment does not automatically produce a plug-compatible ecosystem. You'll identify the information that must cross organizational boundaries and the role of shared models in making that information useful. You'll also choose a concrete next step for participating in the community.

slides.title: Read industry momentum through evidence

bullets.text: An integrated system operating under specific requirements.
Results tied to an evaluated architecture and workload.
Shared tests, models and demonstrations with stated status.

slides.transcript:
Jupiter and the TPU examples show that optical circuit switching can be part of large operational systems. Emerging architectures show a broader set of possibilities. These are different kinds of evidence, and keeping them separate makes the industry's progress easier to assess.

A production deployment demonstrates that a particular organization has integrated and operated a design under its requirements. A research evaluation explores an approach under specified conditions. An interoperability event can test whether implementations work together under agreed scenarios. A planned demonstration is a future activity until it has occurred and produced evidence. The 2026 Summit discussions are useful for understanding priorities and ongoing work, without treating every proposed interface or event as a completed industry standard.

slides.title: Four roles need a shared understanding

figure.alt: Four equally sized panels describe the responsibilities of the source ecosystem roles.
figure.caption: Suppliers, integrators, operators and open communities connect capability to operational use.

slides.transcript:
Technology suppliers develop the optical mechanisms and describe their supported behavior. Systems integrators combine those devices with controllers, software and an overall architecture. Operators turn that architecture into a service, with requirements for capacity, availability, maintenance and recovery. Standards bodies and open communities provide places to develop common descriptions, specifications and tests.

Researchers contribute new ideas and evidence across these layers. The roles are complementary, and one organization may perform several of them. The important question is what must be communicated at each handoff. A supplier's port capability has to mean the same thing to the integrator's software and the operator's validation process. Otherwise, a functional component can still become difficult to deploy or support.

slides.title: Make the handoffs interoperable

figure.alt: A supplier, integrator, operator and standards community exchange capability, connection-state and validation information.
figure.caption: Open specifications and shared control models connect optical components, integrated systems and operational requirements.

entries.text: A component needs a clear description of its capabilities.
Hardware and software must attach the same meaning to a connection.
The reported state must match the service the operator requested.
Requirements and evidence improve the next shared revision.

slides.transcript:
An optical component becomes useful in a deployed system only when the surrounding ecosystem can understand and control it. Start with a technology supplier. The supplier describes the supported ports, optical behavior, and operating limits of the device.

A systems integrator connects those capabilities to orchestration software. The software needs an unambiguous way to describe a requested circuit and to interpret the state that the device reports. Shared data models help both sides attach the same meaning to that information.

An operator requests a connection and checks that the resulting physical state matches the intended service. Hardware capability, software control, and operational evidence must all agree. A working optical component alone does not establish interoperability across an entire system.

Open specifications, reference architectures, and validation work make these handoffs easier to repeat across organizations. Experience from suppliers, integrators, operators, and researchers can then inform the next revision. This is an illustrative workflow, not a particular published OCP interface. The practical opportunity is to contribute clear requirements and evidence at the handoff your team understands best.

slides.title: Make intended and observed connections distinguishable

figure.alt: Device and operator exchange capability, command, request and state information through a shared control model.
figure.caption: Interoperability requires clear capabilities, requested connections and observed operational state.
figure.source_scope: M5 / Building the OCS Ecosystem original video / standardized data models

entries.text: Illustrative contract — not a published API or certification scheme

slides.transcript:
The 2026 interfaces discussion highlights a practical control problem: software needs a consistent way to describe devices, request connectivity and observe state. OpenConfig and YANG provide a modeling approach, while gNMI offers operations such as Get, Set and Subscribe. These names refer to the management interface, not to the optical mechanism itself.

A requested connection and an active connection should be distinguishable. A controller may intend a new circuit while a device is still applying or validating it. Device capabilities can also differ, so software must discover and respect supported behavior. Shared models help make those differences explicit. The cited presentations reflect work in progress; this course does not assert a single current specification version from slides with differing release labels.

slides.title: Automation must verify the physical outcome

bullets.text: Identify the device, peer and supported capabilities.
Compare the actual end-to-end path with the intended service.
Handle mismatches and support a controlled rollback.

slides.transcript:
An automated control request is not the same as an operationally verified path. The zero-touch fabric discussion extends automation across a lifecycle: discover devices and peers, establish intended connectivity, check the resulting path, and respond when observed behavior differs from the plan.

That distinction matters because a logically valid command can still produce an unusable service if cabling, peer identity or optical conditions are wrong. Validation and rollback give the operator a controlled response. Effective automation therefore includes evidence about what actually happened, rather than merely recording that a command was sent. This is a useful contribution area for teams with deployment experience: supply realistic failure cases and clearly defined acceptance checks.

slides.title: Contribute where your team has evidence

figure.alt: Four steps show requirements, evidence, review and improvements to shared specifications and reference designs.
figure.caption: Choose a requirement, bring evidence, collaborate on a shared description, then validate the result.
figure.source_scope: M5 / Building the OCS Ecosystem; participation objective

entries.text: Share a reproducible design or finding
Choose the handoff your team knows; contribute clear requirements and evidence.

slides.transcript:
Participation becomes most useful when it starts with a concrete problem. A supplier can clarify capability limits and provide reproducible measurements. An integrator can identify an ambiguous control behavior. An operator can describe a failure case or a requirement that is missing from a validation plan. A researcher can explain the conditions under which an architecture's benefit holds.

Use the OCP community resources and the white paper to locate the relevant discussions, then bring a clear requirement, example or test. Separate observed behavior from proposed behavior and identify the assumptions others would need to reproduce your result. This helps an open ecosystem improve through evidence that multiple organizations can understand and apply.

slides.title: Open adoption depends on the handoffs
items: Production success and emerging research supply different evidence.
Shared capability and state models help integrate diverse devices.
Operational validation and community contributions turn interfaces into usable systems.
slides.transcript:
The ecosystem story connects everything in the course. A mechanism must meet physical requirements. An architecture must use it in a way that benefits the workload. A control system must express and verify the desired connectivity. An open community can make those requirements and results easier to share.

As you evaluate an OCS proposal, ask where its evidence comes from and which handoff needs further work. Your contribution does not have to be a complete switch or network. A precise requirement, an unambiguous model or a reproducible validation case can help the next organization adopt the technology responsibly.
